overview.text: An mRNA (messenger RNA) vaccine gives some of the body’s cells temporary instructions for making a chosen antigen—a molecule the immune system can recognize. Unlike vaccines that supply a weakened or inactivated germ, mRNA vaccines supply the message for making an antigen. Cells use it to produce a harmless protein piece; immune defenses respond by making antibodies and activating other immune cells, while immune memory can help the body respond faster after later exposure. COVID-19 vaccines provide a familiar example: their mRNA directs cells to produce a piece of SARS-CoV-2’s spike protein. This approach trains immune defenses without requiring the vaccine to contain the whole virus.

key_facts.text: The mRNA carries instructions; it is not the antigen itself. Cells use the instructions to make a protein or protein piece for the immune system to recognize.
For COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the instructed protein piece comes from the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
After cells make the protein piece, they break down and remove the mRNA.
The immune response includes antibodies and other immune cells; immune memory can help the body respond faster if it encounters the same pathogen again.
Researchers have studied mRNA vaccine technology for decades, including for diseases beyond COVID-19.
